## Package overview

Monitoring networks are crucial for understanding how ecosystems respond to environmental change, however, site selection bias (e.g., selecting the most easily accessible or interesting sites) can result in data that are not representative of the landscape. To help researchers and practitioners reduce site selection bias when setting up monitoring networks, we created the R package **siteselectr**. This suite of functions is designed to identify a set of locations that are representative of the multivariate environmental variation present in a landscape (e.g., land use, elevation, road density, climate conditions). By representative, we mean that the selected network of sites covers a fairly large portion of the distribution of possible values of multivariate environmental conditions. The selected sites should represent not just mean or modal conditions, but also extreme minimum and maximum values to capture gradients. 

**siteselectr** is designed to work within common spatial and environmental constraints encountered when designing a monitoring network, and has options for users to prioritize some aspects of environmental variation over others (e.g., perhaps precipitation gradients are more important to some researchers than road density), or to consider only a subset of the landscape (e.g., publicly accessible lands). **siteselectr** can be used at any spatial scale and with any types of environmental data, as the user inputs to the package dictate the resolution and the environmental variation that is selected from.

[The general approach taken when using **siteselectr**:]{.underline}

1.  Define the region in which to select sites.

2.  Characterize the environmental conditions (e.g., elevation, land use, road density) within the region using geospatial data.

3.  Calculate the dissimilarity in the environmental conditions among all possible sites using a modified Mahalanobis distance (MD) algorithm.

4.  Choose a starting location (user input) and then **siteselectr** will select the most dissimilar site to the starting location.

5.  Recalculate the dissimilarity among all non-selected potential sites to the suite of conditions represented in the current network. Iterate until the number of desired sampling sites is reached.

## General Approach

```{r}
library(siteselectr)
library(terra)
library(sf)
```

The **siteselectr** library works with the terra (Hijmans et al. 2025) and sf (Pebesma et al. 2025) packages. Both are used in **siteselectr** to handle raster data (terra) and vectorized shapefiles (sf).

### Define the region

Users should define the region of interest, i.e. the landscape which a monitoring network is meant to represent. The region of interest can be at any spatial scale, and simply needs to be a geospatial boundary within which sites are selected. For example, it could be the outline of a park, a state or province, or any other geospatial area defined by a vectorized shapefile. 

If using an existing shapefile (e.g., ESRI shapefiles, KML), users can load it  `sf::st_read` and project it to their focal coordinate reference system (CRS) using `sf::st_transform` and `sf::st_crs`. with the `sf` package. 

Alternatively, **siteselectr** can create a sampling extent for users based on a point-and-radius approach. The sample_ext() function writes a vectorized point using `sf::st_as_sf` from latitude/longitude coordinates, then projects the point to the desired CRS using an EPSG code. We use the World Geodetic System (WGS) 84 CRS since it's commonly used for GIS analysis and visualization. The sample extent uses a radius value (in meters) supplied by the user in `sf::st_buffer` and uses the Mercator CRS projection which is conformable to a precise geospatial cylindrical calculation surrounding a single central point supplied by the user. Once calculated, the function converts the sampling extent to the supplied CRS. In this example we use 750,000 meters and the coordinates 10.0°N, 12.0°E.

```{r}
sampling_extent <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x=10.0, 
                                           y=12.0, 
                                           radius = 750000, 
                                           crs=4326)
head(sampling_extent)

```

### Characterize environmental conditions

Users should input the environmental conditions in a region as rasterized geospatial data. These should be read in using the `terra` package. Here, rather than using real raster data, we are generating random rasters from a normal distribution to demonstrate package functions. Each raster is generated at a different spatial extent to demonstrate how **siteselectr** handles projections and data organization. Users should input the actual environmental data they want to have represented by their selected sites. 

```{r}
var1 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(900, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 30, ncol = 30),
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var2 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(625, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 25, ncol = 25),
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var3 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(625, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 25, ncol = 25),
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var4 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(1500, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 750, ncol = 750),
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var5 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(1500, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 750, ncol = 750),
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
```

Let's visualize the sampling extent on one of the simulated rasters. 


```{r}
plot(var1) ; lines(sampling_extent, col='red', lwd=3)
```

#### Align geospatial layers

Often, environmental data stored in rasters will not be at the same extent as our region of interest (i.e., some cells in the raster are outside our sampling extent). The main function in the **siteselectr** package, `site_select`, uses `terra::mask` to ensure any cells outside the sampling extent are excluded - we demonstrate what this looks like here:

```{r}
var1_mask <- terra::trim(terra::mask(var1, sampling_extent))
plot(var1_mask)
```

Use `rast_collect` to take a set of rasters and place them in a usable list.

```{r}
r_list <- siteselectr::rast_collect(var1, var2, var3, var4, var5)
```

Use `rast_match` to resample the raster list to the same extent, resolution, and CRS. `rast_match` uses `terra::project` and `sf::st_transform` to align the sampling extent and the raster data. This step is necessary to calculate a distance matrix that's spatially the same as our raster data. The raster list is projected to match a reference raster - we've arbitrarily chosen the fourth raster layer to be our reference. The extent should be the sampling extent defined above.

```{r}
r_resampled <- siteselectr::rast_match(rast_list = r_list,
                                       reference_layer = r_list[[4]],
                                       extent = sampling_extent)
str(r_resampled)
```

As a final data preparation step, **siteselectr** uses `rast_stack` to convert the resampled list of rasters into a single georeferenced object, a raster stack, then realigns the its extent and masks the stack to our sampling extent. The extent and resolution of the rasters are harmonized to ensure that the Mahalanobis calculation matches their geospatial information exactly. If the rasters are not projected to the exact same extent and resolution for each data preparation step, the function will still produce values, however, the distance values will not actually be meaningful when applied to the landscape.

```{r}
r_stack <- siteselectr::rast_stack(r_resampled, sampling_extent)

names(r_stack) <- c("Raster 1", 
                    "Raster 2", 
                    "Raster 3", 
                    "Raster4", 
                    "Raster5")

plot(r_stack)

```


### Select sites

We now have a sampling extent and a stack of rasters - the necessary components needed to run `site_select` which is the main function of **siteselectr**. `site_select` is a wrapper function which takes a raster stack along with a *latitude* and *longitude* for the starting location. It then returns a vector with the indices of the selected sites, up to some number set by the user. *num* refers to number of cells to select. The desired number of cells accounts for the starting location. So if we set *num* to 15, it will return 15 sites and one of those will be our starting latitude and longitude that's entered into the `site_select` function.

```{r}
sites <-
  siteselectr::site_select(
    long = 12,
    lat = 10,
    num = 15,
    stack = r_stack
  )
print(sites)
```

We can visualize our sites by converting the selected cells into geographic coordinates.

```{r}
site_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], sites)
plot(r_stack[[1]])
points(site_xy, col = 'red', pch = 19)
```

```{r}
print(site_xy)
```


#### Underlying calculations of `site_select`

Let's break down `site_select` so users understand what is happening within the function. Note that users could stop at the step above, and this section is meant to be instructive so that users understand the logic behind how sites were selected. 

First, `site_select` converts the raster stack into a matrix. Then, the first layer of the raster stack is copied and its values removed to be used as a geographic reference to choose cells and convert them to coordinates.

```{r}
rast_data <- as.matrix(r_stack)
ref_layer <- r_stack[[1]]
values(ref_layer) <- NA
```

We can build the distance matrix using Mahalanobis distance (MD) calculation on the raster stack matrix. Mahalanobis is equipped for multivariate environmental data that exhibits correlated features and can return a matrix that corresponds to geospatial points. The Mahalanobis distance is calculated as:

`d^2 = (x_{ijk} - μ)' Σ⁻¹(x_{ijk} - μ)`

where k is vector of environmental values at a given latitude(i) and longitude(j), μ is the mean vector across the raster layers -- transposed to align with the inverse covariance matrix; Σ⁻¹ is the inverse of the covariance matrix, which adjusts for correlations among focal variables. This results in a scalar metric at each cell that reflects multivariate dissimilarity across all raster layers at once (Etherington, 2021; De Maesschalck, Jouan-Rimbaud, and Massart, 2000).

We created the covariance matrix using the `cov` function, allowing for missing values by setting 'use' to `pairwise.complete.obs` -- [this is essential since NA values contribute to the spatial integrity of the raster data and cannot be removed]{.underline}. We added a diagonal of small values (0.01) to regularize the matrix which helps limit singularity issues between colinear data. We calculated the center mean for the Mahalanobis calculation using `colMeans` on the raster data, ignoring NA values. `site_select` uses the `mahalanobis` function - its parameters being the matrix of the raster stack data, center mean, and covariance matrix to produce the initial distance matrix.

We wrap this process in the function, `rast_distance`, which measures the dissimilarity between one cell to another relative to the mean distribution of the raster stack.

```{r}
distance_matrix <- siteselectr::rast_distance(data = rast_data)
summary(distance_matrix)
```

We can use `heat_distance` to visualize the dissimilarity in our matrix. The highest dissimilar area will be chosen first. `heat_distance` maps an empty raster of NA values, and then inserts the distance matrix values into the empty cells.

```{r}
heat_map <- siteselectr::heat_distance(raster_stack = r_stack, 
                             dist_mat = distance_matrix)
plot(heat_map)
```

We now have a matrix of distance values, where each cell corresponds to a geographic location and its environmental variation. Next, we'll use `max_cell` to select the most dissimilar cell in the distance matrix.

```{r}
max <- siteselectr::max_cell(distance_matrix = distance_matrix)
print(max)
```

`site_select` combines the two cells (the starting location and max distance site) into a usable format using `cell_combine` and visualize them on our dissimilarity map (e.g., `heat_distance` function). To wrap the coordinates used to build the sampling approach into a usable object we use `cell_wrap` which converts our starting location into a set of georeferenced coordinates and uses `terra::cellFromXY` into a single cell value that corresponds to our sampling extent.

```{r}
cell1 <- siteselectr::cell_wrap(x = 12,
                                y = 10,
                                raster_stack = r_stack)
cells <- siteselectr::cell_combine(cell1, max)
print(cells)
```

We can quickly view these cells below. Notice the starting location we used to create the sampling extent is in the center, and the max distance site is placed in the cell with the highest dissimilarity.

```{r}
cells_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], cells)
plot(heat_map)
points(cells_xy, col = 'red', pch = 19)
```

These 2 sites are the basis for automating the remaining code in the `site_select` function. The first Mahalanobis calculation represents the dissimilarity across the entire environmental gradient each cell in relation to every other cell of the raster stack. This is represented by the product of `max_cell`. Every following site selection must account for the environmental variation minus the cells that were already chosen. An approach that we include in the `new_distance` function wrapped inside `site_select`.

`new_distance` uses the Mahalanobis equation - same as `rast_distance`. While `rast_distance` measures the variability in one dataset (our raster data), `new_distance` creates two datasets - a available group which is the original distance matrix produced from `rast_distance` and the comparison group, which is the available group with the values of selected cells replaced with NA values which preserves the spatial integrity of the matrix. Then, instead of calculating the dissimilarity between every cell to each other, `new_distance` measures the dissimilarity between every cell not selected yet (comparison group) to every possible cell (available group) simultaneously.

```{r}
new_matrix <- siteselectr::new_distance(rast_data, cells)
summary(new_matrix)
```

Now choose another site with `max_cell`. Before using `max_cell` we create an empty raster that is filled with our new matrix values. This avoids any spatial irregularities. We combine this with our existing list of cells and plot.

```{r}
ref <- r_stack[[1]]
tmp.r <- as.matrix(ref)
tmp.r[!is.na(tmp.r)] <- NA
tmp.r[-c(cells)] <- new_matrix

max.diff <- which.max(tmp.r)

cells <- c(cells, max.diff)
print(cells)
```

Let's automate this approach in a for-loop, which is what `site_select` does when we give the number of sites to select. Here we chose 15 iterations - we will receive 15 sites, one of which is our starting location we used to create the sampling extent. For each iteration, `site_select` updates the cells list, thereby ensuring an updated distance matrix in the next round of site selection.

```{r}
num = 12

for (i in 1:num) {
  nd <- siteselectr::new_distance(rast_data, cells)
  tmp.r <- as.matrix(ref)
  tmp.r[!is.na(tmp.r)] <- NA
  tmp.r[-c(cells)] <- nd
  
  mc <- siteselectr::max_cell(tmp.r)
  
  cells <- siteselectr::cell_combine(cells, mc)
}

print(cells)
```

```{r}
final_sites <- terra::xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], cells)
plot(r_stack[[1]])
points(final_sites, col = 'red', pch = 19)
```

We can use `site_val` to pull the cell values from the original raster data for each field site. `site_val` uses `terra::extract`, then converts the product to a matrix which can be used to assess how well `site_select` chose sites that represent the environmental variability of our data.

```{r}
cell_values <- siteselectr::site_val(final_sites, r_stack)
print(cell_values)
```

With these values let's check if our sites are representative of variation across our raster data. To do this, we have developed two tools which might be helpful for users to assess their final output. (1) To view the collinearity between variables at site locations, `vis_cor` creates a correlation plot that shows the correlation between raster values at each site. This might be useful to view how separated correlated variables are at site locations (e.g., urban cover, population density, and temperature).

```{r}
cor_plot <- siteselectr::vis_cor(cell_values)
```

Each cell is a site, and at each site the value is either collinear (red) or noncollinear (blue) between the corresponding variables. `vis_cor` returns a table of correlations as well. Using `vis_cor` might be favorable so users know which variables can and can't be statistically separated a priori.

\(2\) `vis_rep` takes the cell values from `site_val` and plots two raster layers to compare where in their distribution our site values lie. The goal of **siteselectr** is to represent environmental space evenly during site selection - especially covering the maximum and minimum values (i.e., avoiding mean-driven selection) so it is favorable to have sites that occupy the entirety of each layer. `vis_rep` uses the cell values, raster stack, and the numerical value for the position of each layer to compare. Here we compare how well cell values are distributed between layers 1 and 2.

```{r}
# vis_rep(values=cell_values, stack=r_stack, layer1 = 1, layer2 = 2)

plot(r_stack[[1]], r_stack[[2]], col="lightgray")
points(cell_values[, 1], cell_values[, 2], col="red", pch=19, cex=1.0)
```

## Weighted Approach

The Mahalanobis distance equation is designed to treat all parameters equally. However, a common practice in ecological monitoring is to focus on one or a few variables while still accounting for other multivariate influence. **siteselectr** offers a modified version of our general approach, `site_select_wt`, which weights specific raster layers entered into the Mahalanobis calculation. The Mahalanobis calculation used in `site_select_wt` is modified for our use based the `wmahalanobis` function in the **WMDB** package (Wu, 2012).

Like `site_select`, the `site_select_wt` function requires a latitude and longitude to create a sampling extent, the number of desired sites, and a raster stack - the raster stack is created using the same functions described above. In addition, `site_select_wt` requires the layers in the raster stack to weight. For instance, entering `weighted_layer = c(1,3)` like we do below, will put a weight on the first and third layer of the raster stack. *magnitude* refers to the magnitude of weight to place on the focal layer(s). All layers are weighted by 0.001 by default - we typically start weighting layers by 0.1, with \>0.5 being considered a large magnitude to apply. In our example below, we weight the first and third layer by 0.5. 

```{r}
weighted_cells <- siteselectr::site_select_wt(
  long = 10,
  lat = 9.5,
  num = 12,
  stack = r_stack,
  weighted_layer = 1,
  magnitude = 0.8
)
print(weighted_cells)
```

`site_select_wt` functions similar to `site_select`: cells are iteratively selected based on their maximum dissimilarity from the current set of selected and unselected cells. The key difference is that `site_select_wt` allows specific raster layers to be up‑weighted during the Mahalanobis distance calculation.

Weights are applied by constructing a diagonal matrix whose entries correspond to the user‑specified magnitude for selected variables. These weights scale the variables prior to the covariance inversion, increasing the influence of the chosen layers on the resulting distance metric. As a result, cells that are extreme in the weighted variables contribute more strongly to the Mahalanobis distance.

During site selection, the algorithm still identifies the most dissimilar (i.e., environmentally extreme) cells in the weighted Mahalanobis space. These typically correspond to areas with high variation in the focal variable(s) (e.g., elevation, precipitation). However, because the Mahalanobis distance inherently rescales all variables and accounts for covariance structure, the weighting does not dominate the selection entirely. Instead, it biases the selection toward the focal variable(s) while still maintaining a multivariate balance across all layers.

```{r}
weighted_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], weighted_cells)

plot(r_stack[[4]])
points(weighted_xy, col = 'red', pch = 19)
```

## Filter Approach

**siteselectr** provides a function for selecting representative field sites under geographic constraints---a common limitation that researchers might face, such as choosing field sites within public or other accessible land in vectorized polygon format. Filtering can be done before or after calculating the multivariate dissimilarity among cells. The output between the two might be similar and in both, cells will be masked to the filter polygon. Users might favor filtering before the Mahalanobis distance calculation if they are interested in the dissimilarity among cells exclusively within the spatial constraint. Filtering after the distance calculation may be more appropriate if the intent is to understand measured outcomes across the entire region of interest. Sites might be similar between the two approaches.

Let's try out `site_select_fil`, which uses the same framework as `site_select` but either masks the cells before the distance calculation, or directly masks the distance matrix to the filter polygon.

First, let's simulate a new set of rasters and create a set of polygons for the filter layer.

```{r}
# simulate data 
var_list <- list()
n <- 7

ext <- sampling_extent <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 25, y = 25, 
                          radius = 1500000, 
                          crs = 4326)

var1 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(3600, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 60, ncol = 60), 
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var2 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(6400, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 80, ncol = 80), 
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var3 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(6400, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 80, ncol = 80), 
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var4 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(3600, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                           nrow = 60, ncol = 60), 
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")
var5 <- terra::rast(matrix(rnorm(3600, mean = 0, sd = 1), 
                           nrow = 60, ncol = 60), 
                    crs = "EPSG:4326")

r_list <- siteselectr::rast_collect(var1, var2, var3, var4, var5)

r_resampled <- siteselectr::rast_match(rast_list = r_list,
                          reference_layer = r_list[[1]],
                          extent = ext)

r_stack <- siteselectr::rast_stack(r_resampled, extent = ext)

# simulate polygons to mask rasters (our filter)
f1 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 25, y = 25, 200000, crs = 4326)
f2 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 25, y = 30, 200000, crs = 4326)
f3 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 20, y = 23, 200000, crs = 4326)
f4 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 30, y = 16, 200000, crs = 4326)
f5 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 30, y = 28, 200000, crs = 4326)
f6 <- siteselectr::sample_ext(x = 17, y = 32, 200000, crs = 4326)

fil <- rbind(f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6)

plot(r_stack[[1]])
lines(ext, col = 'red', lwd = 3)
lines(fil, col = 'red', lwd = 2)
```

With a raster stack and single shapefile that contains polygons which will be used to mask the raster data, we're ready to run `site_select_fil`.

```{r}
fil_after <- siteselectr::site_select_fil(
  long = 25,
  lat = 25,
  num = 12,
  stack = r_stack,
  filter = fil,
  type = "after"
)

fil_before <- siteselectr::site_select_fil(
  long = 25,
  lat = 25,
  num = 12,
  stack = r_stack,
  filter = fil,
  type = "before"
)
```

We can view our sites on the filtered cells - some of them will be the same or similar between a priori or a posteriori filtering.

```{r}
after_xy <- xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], fil_after)
before_xy <- xyFromCell(r_stack[[1]], fil_before)

plot(mask(r_stack[[1]], fil))
points(after_xy,
       pch = 19,
       col = "cyan",
       cex = 2)
points(before_xy,
       pch = 4,
       col = "red",
       cex = 2)
```
